interpretations of the Act itself. * * *
There are, however, reasons to doubt that the case should be 
read so broadly. Indeed, the Court has not lived up to the notion that 
the APA should be hterally or narrowly interpreted—even in some of 
the very opinions that have given lip service to the idea that courts 
are not free to impose rulemaking procedures on their own initiative. 
In Vermont Yankee itself, while denouncing judicial imposition of 
extra-statutory cross-examination obhgations, the Court also 
directed that, on remand, the court of appeals must evaluate the 
vahdity of the rule by determining whether the agency’s 
contemporaneous explanation for its decision is “sustainable on the 
administrative record made.” * * * [T]he practice of reviewing a rule 
on the administrative record was a judicial invention, not a practice 
contemplated by the drafters of the APA.
Similarly, in [Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association, 135 S.Ct. 
1199 (2015), discussed in this chapter], the Court disapproved a line 
of D.C. Circuit cases that had held that an agency must use notice- 
and-comment rulemaking in order to replace an interpretive rule 
with another interpretive rule. In her opinion for a unanimous Court, 
Justice Sotomayor declared that the lower court’s view, which did not 
purport to derive this requirement from the APA or any other statute, 
was incompatible with Vermont Yankee. At the same time, in the 
course of summarizing the steps that the APA does require in a 
notice-and-comment proceeding, she remarked that “[a]n agency 
must consider and respond to significant comments received during 
the period for pubhc comment.” The text of the APA, however, says 
nothing about a duty to respond to comments.
I do not mean to suggest that Vermont Yankee has become a dead 
letter. However, the Court has left itself room to maneuver. What 
seems to have happened is that, when the Court disagrees with an 
alleged procedural requirement, it deploys Vermont Yankee as a 
justification for its rejection of the argument. On the other hand, 
where the Court does agree with the APA claim, it simply adopts the 
proposed interpretation with no mention of a potential Vermont 
Yankee problem. For example, when a unanimous Court [in Long 
Island Care at Home} endorsed the ‘logical outgrowth” test for 
variance between the proposed and final rule, it did not mention any 
Vermont Yankee problem.
Ronald M. Levin, The Evolving APA and the Originalist Challenge, 97 Ch i.- 
Ke n t L. Re v . 7, 20-22 (2022).
Note that then-Judge Kavanaugh’s comments in American Radio Relay 
League did not stop him from joining the Supreme Court majority’s application 
of State Farm in Ohio v. EP A, 144 S.Ct. 2040 (2024), discussed earlier in this 
chapter.
